11000:
To mutilate something means to damage it severely — usually by cutting, tearing, or forcibly removing a part of it — so that it is left in a disfigured, incomplete, or unrecognizable state.

The single most important thing to understand about this word is that it is not just about hurting or damaging something. It is about destroying the wholeness or integrity of something in a violent, drastic way. When something is mutilated, a piece of it is gone, ruined, or so badly disfigured that the thing can never fully return to what it was.

Think of it in three parts:

1. Something whole exists.
A body, a statue, a document, an animal — something that has a complete, intact form.

2. A violent or severe action happens.
Cutting, tearing, hacking, ripping, crushing — something forceful and destructive occurs.

3. The result is disfigured and incomplete.
A part is missing, destroyed, or so badly mangled that the original form is permanently compromised.

That three-step picture is what "mutilate" captures.

This is a strong, serious word. It sits far beyond words like "damage," "harm," or "hurt." Consider this scale:

  • Scratch → very minor surface damage
  • Injure → hurt, but likely recoverable
  • Damage → something is broken or impaired
  • Mutilate → severe, grotesque, often irreversible destruction of part of something

When you say something was mutilated, you are telling the listener that what happened was drastic, shocking, and permanent. The word carries a heavy emotional weight. It almost always makes people uncomfortable, because it conjures an image of something that has been made unrecognizable or incomplete in a disturbing way.

On the human or animal body

This is the most common use. When a body — human or animal — has a limb severed, a face badly disfigured, or body parts destroyed by violence or an accident, we say it was mutilated.

"The victim's body had been mutilated beyond recognition."
"His hand was mutilated in the factory accident, with two fingers torn off completely."
"Poachers mutilate rhinoceroses by cutting off their horns."

Notice that in each case, the person or animal is not simply hurt — something has been violently removed or destroyed, leaving the body permanently and grotesquely altered.

On objects

You can mutilate an object too. A coin that has been badly defaced, a statue with its limbs broken off, a painting slashed to pieces — all of these can be described as mutilated.

"Vandals mutilated the ancient sculpture by smashing its face and hands."
"The book was so old and damaged that its pages were mutilated beyond reading."

Here, the idea is the same: the object has lost part of its form or integrity in a severe, damaging way.

On a text or piece of work

You can also use "mutilate" in a more figurative sense when referring to creative or written work. If someone cuts out large, essential portions of a manuscript, script, or piece of music — altering it so severely that it no longer resembles the original — they can be said to have mutilated it.

"The director mutilated the original novel by removing entire subplots and changing the ending."
"The censors mutilated the article, cutting out over half of its content."

This use is less graphic but carries the same idea: something essential has been removed, and the work is now incomplete and disfigured.
What Makes It Different from Similar Words

Mutilate vs. Injure: To injure means to cause harm, but injury often implies the possibility of recovery. A mutilated thing is typically damaged in a way that is permanent and severe. You injure your ankle; you do not "mutilate" it. But if your hand is destroyed in an explosion and fingers are lost, that is mutilation.

Mutilate vs. Destroy: To destroy something is to eliminate it entirely — it ceases to exist. To mutilate something is to damage it so severely that it is disfigured or incomplete, but it still exists in that broken state. A mutilated body is still a body. A destroyed building is rubble. The horror of mutilation is partly that the damaged thing remains — visibly, disturbingly incomplete.

Mutilate vs. Disfigure: These are close. To disfigure means to spoil the appearance of something, usually a face or body. Mutilate is broader and stronger — it includes disfigurement but also emphasises the violent removal or severe destruction of a part. All mutilation causes disfigurement, but not all disfigurement is mutilation.

Mutilate vs. Damage: To damage is a neutral, everyday word for making something worse or less functional. Mutilate is far more extreme and always implies something shocking, violent, and irreversible.

You will very often see "mutilate" in the passive voice: mutilated. This is because the focus is usually on the thing that suffered the damage, not on who did it.

"The soldier was mutilated by a landmine."
"The painting was found mutilated in the gallery."

Mutilation can be both deliberate (done on purpose, often with cruelty) and accidental (the result of a terrible accident). The word itself does not judge the intent — it only describes the nature of the damage.

Deliberate: "The attacker mutilated his victim with a knife."
Accidental: "His arm was mutilated when it got caught in the machine."

"Mutilate" is not a casual or everyday word. You would not use it lightly. It belongs in serious contexts — news reports about violence, medical or legal descriptions, literary writing, or discussions of art and censorship. When someone uses this word, they are signalling that what happened was severe, graphic, and significant. It is a word that demands the reader's full attention.

To mutilate something is to damage it so severely — usually through violent cutting, tearing, or removal of a part — that it is left permanently disfigured, incomplete, and altered beyond its original form.
11001:
Mutilation is the serious, severe, and often permanent damaging or destruction of a body — human or animal — in a way that cuts off, tears away, or badly disfigures a part of it. The damage is not minor. It goes far beyond a scratch, a bruise, or even a deep cut. Mutilation means something significant has been destroyed, removed, or ruined beyond normal repair.

Think of it this way: if someone breaks their arm, that is an injury. If someone loses their arm entirely — or has it so badly destroyed that it can never function again — that edges into mutilation. The keyword is severe and lasting destruction of form or function.

The word has two things at its heart:

1. A body part is involved.
Mutilation almost always refers to flesh, limbs, organs, or the physical structure of a living (or once-living) being. It is deeply physical.

2. The damage is extreme.
It is not just harm — it is disfigurement, amputation, or destruction of a body part. After mutilation, the body is noticeably and seriously altered in a bad way. Something is missing, mangled, or ruined.
What Kinds of Situations Use This Word?

In Violence and Crime

When someone is attacked and body parts are cut off, torn away, or badly destroyed, news reports and legal documents describe this as mutilation. A victim of an extremely brutal attack whose face, hands, or other parts have been severely disfigured has suffered mutilation. Courts treat mutilation as a very serious matter — it is often listed separately from regular assault because of how severe and permanent the harm is.

In War

Mutilation appears in accounts of warfare — both when soldiers are wounded so severely that limbs are lost, and in the darker historical practice of enemies mutilating the bodies of the fallen. This is considered one of the most disturbing acts in conflict, which is why international laws of war specifically prohibit the mutilation of bodies.

In Medicine and Surgery — a Special Note

This is important: not all removal of body parts is mutilation. When a surgeon amputates a leg to save a patient's life, that is medicine, not mutilation — even though a limb is removed. The word "mutilation" carries the idea of wrongful, unnecessary, or harmful destruction. Context and intention matter enormously.

However, if someone deliberately harms their own body in an extreme way without medical necessity, that is often called self-mutilation. This is a recognized and serious topic in mental health.

In Ritual and Cultural Practices

The word is used — sometimes controversially — to describe certain traditional practices that permanently alter the body. The most well-known example is the term Female Genital Mutilation (FGM), which is the official term used by the World Health Organization for the practice of partially or fully removing female genitalia for non-medical reasons. The use of the word "mutilation" here is deliberate — it signals that the international community views this as harmful and wrong, not a neutral cultural act.

In Animal Contexts

When animals — livestock, pets, or wildlife — have body parts cut off or severely damaged, especially unnecessarily, this is also called mutilation. It is considered a serious form of animal cruelty.

Beyond the Literal Body — Extended Use

While the primary meaning is physical, "mutilation" is sometimes used in a figurative sense. For example, if someone edits a great piece of writing so carelessly and destructively that it no longer resembles the original or has lost all its quality, one might say the text was mutilated. The idea here is the same — something was damaged so severely and irreversibly that it is now a ruined version of what it once was. This figurative use is less common but perfectly valid.

Mutilation is not a neutral word. It carries strong negative weight. When you use it or hear it, it signals:

  • Severity — this was not minor damage.
  • Permanence — something cannot simply heal back to normal.
  • Wrongness — there is almost always a moral dimension. Mutilation is something that should not have happened.
  • Horror or distress — the word tends to create a visceral reaction in the reader or listener because it points to something deeply disturbing about the destruction of a body.

This is why writers, journalists, and legal professionals choose this word carefully. It is a strong, serious word, and using it tells your audience that what happened was grave.

To sharpen your understanding, here is how mutilation sits differently from related words:

  • Injury — broad term; even a sprained ankle is an injury. Mutilation is a specific, extreme form of injury.
  • Wound — refers to a cut or tear in the body; a wound can heal. Mutilation implies permanent, severe disfigurement.
  • Disfigurement — close in meaning, but disfigurement focuses on the appearance being ruined (e.g., a scarred face). Mutilation focuses more on the destruction or removal of body parts. The two often overlap.
  • Amputation — the clinical, neutral medical term for removing a limb. Mutilation is the charged, morally weighted version of the same act when it happens outside a medical context, or in a harmful way.
  • Dismemberment — refers specifically to the cutting off or separation of limbs or body parts. Dismemberment is one type of mutilation. All dismemberment is mutilation, but not all mutilation is dismemberment (e.g., severe burns that destroy a face are mutilation without dismemberment).
How to Use It in Sentences

• "The soldier survived the explosion, but the mutilation of his hand meant he would never regain full use of it."
  • "The authorities condemned the mutilation of the animals found on the farm."
  • "International law strictly prohibits the mutilation of fallen soldiers during wartime."
  • "The editor's changes were so reckless that the author described them as the mutilation of her novel."

Mutilation is the severe, often permanent, and typically wrongful destruction, removal, or disfigurement of a body part — physical damage so extreme that the body is left in a fundamentally altered and diminished state.
11002:
A mutineer is a person who openly rebels against the authority of their leader or commander — specifically from within an organized, structured group like a military unit, a ship's crew, or a prison.

The key word here is within. A mutineer is not an outsider attacking a system. They are an insider — a soldier, a sailor, a guard — who is supposed to follow orders but instead turns against the people commanding them.

Imagine you are a sailor on a large ship. The captain is in charge. You and the rest of the crew are expected to follow the captain's orders without question. That is the rule of the sea.

Now imagine the captain is cruel. He starves the crew, beats them, and makes unreasonable demands. One day, you and a group of fellow sailors have had enough. You rise up together, seize control of the ship, and remove the captain from power.

In that moment, you have committed mutiny — and you are now a mutineer.

So, simply put: a mutineer is someone who participates in a revolt against authority within an organized group.
What Makes Someone a Mutineer — The Three Key Elements

For someone to be called a mutineer, three things must generally be true:

1. They belong to a structured group with a clear chain of command.
Mutineers are always part of a system — an army, a navy, a crew, a prison. There has to be an "above" and a "below." Mutineers come from below and act against those above them.

2. They actively defy or overthrow their commanders.
A mutineer doesn't just think about rebelling or complain quietly. They act. They refuse orders, take control by force, lock up the officers, or do whatever it takes to seize power from the leaders. It is an open, defiant act.

3. They usually act as part of a group.
Mutiny is almost always a collective act. One person alone who disobeys an order is typically called insubordinate or a deserter. When a group of people rise up together against their commanders, those people are mutineers.
The Two Sides of a Mutineer

This word carries a fascinating tension. Whether a mutineer is seen as a villain or a hero depends entirely on whose side you are on.

From the authority's point of view, a mutineer is a criminal, a dangerous traitor who destroys order and discipline. Historically, mutiny was one of the most serious crimes a soldier or sailor could commit — often punishable by death. The thinking was: if soldiers can overthrow their commanders whenever they feel like it, no army or navy can function.

From the mutineer's point of view (or from the eyes of people who sympathize with them), mutineers can be seen as brave people who stood up against injustice, cruelty, or an abuse of power. If a captain is a tyrant, is it wrong to remove him? Many mutineers believed they had no other choice.

This is why the word "mutineer" doesn't carry a single, fixed moral judgment. It describes the act, not whether the act was right or wrong.

Historically, the word is most at home in naval and military settings. Ships at sea were isolated, with the captain having almost absolute power over the crew — which made the possibility of mutiny very real and very dramatic. This is why so many famous mutinies happened at sea.

Today, the word is also used in:

  • Military contexts — soldiers or prisoners who revolt against commanding officers
  • Fiction and film — it's a favourite word in pirate stories, war films, and historical dramas
  • Loosely, in everyday speech — sometimes people humorously call a group of friends or colleagues "mutineers" if they jokingly refuse to follow someone's lead (e.g., "I told everyone we were going for pizza, but the mutineers voted for burgers")

The Mutiny on the Bounty (1789) is the most famous mutiny in history. Sailors aboard the British ship HMS Bounty, led by Fletcher Christian, rose up against their captain, William Bligh, whom they considered harsh and tyrannical. They set Bligh adrift on a small boat and took over the ship. Every one of those sailors was a mutineer.

The Indian Sepoy Mutiny (1857) involved Indian soldiers serving in the British colonial army who mutinied against their British officers, sparking a massive uprising. These soldiers were called mutineers by the British, but many Indians viewed them as freedom fighters.

These examples show how the same word — mutineer — can mean "criminal" to one group and "hero" to another.
How It Differs from Similar Words

• A rebel is anyone who resists authority in any context — political, social, personal. A mutineer is a specific type of rebel: always within an organized, hierarchical group.
  • A traitor betrays their country or group, often secretly or by siding with an enemy. A mutineer acts openly and internally — they're not sneaking information to an enemy; they're directly overthrowing their own leaders.
  • A revolutionary wants to change an entire political system or society. A mutineer's goal is usually narrower — to remove or defy a specific set of commanders, not necessarily to change the whole world.
  • A rioter takes part in civil unrest in public. A mutineer acts within a controlled, closed group structure.

• "The mutineers locked the officers below deck and steered the ship toward the island."
  • "He was tried as a mutineer and faced execution for leading the revolt against the general."
  • "History remembers the mutineers not as criminals, but as men who refused to accept injustice."

A mutineer is a person — typically a soldier, sailor, or member of an organized group — who openly revolts against their own commanders or leaders from within that group, either out of desperation, a sense of injustice, or a desire for power.
11003:
When you describe someone or something as mutinous, you are saying they are openly defying, resisting, or rebelling against a figure of authority over them — and not just quietly grumbling or feeling unhappy, but doing so in a bold, forceful, and potentially dangerous way.

The central idea is: a person in authority gives a command, and instead of obeying, the mutinous person refuses openly — or goes even further and attempts to overthrow that authority entirely.
The full spectrum of its meaning

Mutinous works across a spectrum of intensity, from deadly serious to quietly figurative.

At its most intense, it describes people who are in an active state of revolt — they have already refused orders and are taking aggressive action to overthrow whoever commands them. "The mutinous crew seized the ship and locked the captain below deck."

In the middle, it describes people on the dangerous edge of revolt — they haven't fully acted yet, but the situation is threatening to explode. "The general could see his troops growing mutinous after months without pay or food."

At its mildest (and most figurative), it describes a fierce, defiant attitude in everyday, non-military situations — applied to looks, expressions, moods, or even private thoughts. "She gave her manager a mutinous glare when he announced she would have to work the weekend."

Crucially, all three shades carry the same flavor: this is never quiet resentment or passive sadness. Mutinous always signals something bold, visible, and resistant — defiance that is out in the open, not buried inside.
How it differs from similar words

Several words are close in meaning, and understanding the differences sharpens your grasp of "mutinous" considerably.

Disobedient is mild and general. A child who won't tidy their room is disobedient. Mutinous carries far greater weight — it implies serious, organized, and potentially dangerous defiance, the kind that threatens the entire structure of authority, not just a single rule.

Rebellious is closer, but rebellious often describes a broad personality trait or a wide social revolt (against a system, a culture, society at large). Mutinous is more specific and direct — it points to defiance within an existing chain of command, by people who are supposed to be under someone's orders, turning sharply against that very person.

Seditious is close too, but it specifically refers to trying to overthrow a government through speech or writing. Mutinous is more immediate and physical — it is about action and direct confrontation, not just provocative words.
Can it describe things other than people?

Yes, and this is an important part of the word's range. Mutinous can describe:

A mood — "A mutinous mood spread through the factory floor after the announcement."
A look or expression — "He shot his father a mutinous look across the table."
A group — "The mutinous soldiers refused to advance."
Even inner thoughts or feelings — "Mutinous thoughts rose within her as she listened to the speech."

When used for looks, moods, or feelings, "mutinous" vividly conveys that someone is barely containing their defiance — that rebellion is simmering right at the surface, ready to boil over.
How strong a word is it?

It is a powerful word. You would not use it for mild frustration or ordinary stubbornness. When a writer or speaker reaches for "mutinous," they want you to feel the danger and gravity of the situation — the sense that authority is being seriously challenged, that things could spiral out of control. The word carries a dramatic charge.

Rebellious, defiant, insubordinate, insurgent, unruly, disaffected, refractory.

Of these, insubordinate is the closest match in professional or workplace settings (flatly refusing orders from a superior). Insurgent matches the military and political intensity of the word. Defiant is slightly milder and more general-purpose.

Mutiny (noun) — the act of revolt itself. "The crew staged a mutiny."
Mutineer (noun) — the person who participates in a mutiny. "The mutineers were put on trial."
Mutiny (verb) — to carry out the revolt. "The soldiers mutinied against their commanding officer."
Mutinously (adverb) — in a mutinous manner. "She stared at him mutinously and folded her arms."

In a military or naval setting: "The mutinous regiment refused to march and demanded the general's resignation."

In a workplace setting: "The mutinous employees drafted a collective letter condemning the new policy."

In a personal/emotional context: "A mutinous feeling welled up inside him every time his boss took credit for his work."

In describing someone's expression: "The child's mutinous pout told her parents the argument was far from over."
A simple image to anchor it in your memory

Picture a ship's captain shouting orders at his crew — and the crew slowly crossing their arms, turning their backs, advancing toward him. That image — bold, organized, dangerous defiance by people who are supposed to follow commands but are now turning against the very person in charge — is the heart of what "mutinous" means. Carry that picture with you, and the word will never escape you.
11004:
A mutiny is when a group of people who are supposed to follow orders from a commander or authority figure openly refuse to obey — or violently turn against — that very authority. It is a collective act of rebellion from within a chain of command, carried out by the people who were originally serving under it.

The single most important thing to understand about mutiny is this: it comes from the inside. The people carrying out a mutiny are not outsiders or enemies attacking from outside. They are the soldiers, sailors, or subordinates who were already part of the group, who were supposed to be loyal, and who chose to revolt from within.

Imagine you are a captain of a ship. You have 50 sailors working under you. One day, your sailors have had enough — maybe because of your cruelty, unfair treatment, or terrible decisions. So they band together, overpower you, lock you in a cabin, and take control of the ship themselves. That is a mutiny.

Notice a few things in that example:

  • It wasn't one person acting alone. It was a group acting together.
  • These were not strangers or enemies. They were your own crew — people under your command.
  • They didn't just complain quietly. They actively defied or overthrew the authority above them.

Those three things — a group, from within the ranks, actively defying authority — are the heart of what mutiny means.

Mutiny is most at home in settings that have a strict, formal hierarchy — where the rules of obedience are not optional but mandatory, and where breaking those rules is considered a serious crime. The most classic settings are:

  • Naval/military: Sailors revolting against a ship's captain, or soldiers refusing to follow the orders of their officers. This is where the word has been used most throughout history.
  • Military units on land: Troops collectively refusing to carry out orders, or turning their weapons against their own commanding officers.
  • Prisons: Inmates collectively rising up against prison guards or administration.
  • Any strict institutional command structure where people are bound by duty to obey.
What Makes Mutiny Different from Similar Words

It is easy to confuse mutiny with similar words like rebellion, revolt, or riot. Here is how mutiny stands apart:

  • A rebellion or revolt can be carried out by anyone against any authority — citizens against a government, for example. The people rebelling were never necessarily part of that authority's force.
  • A mutiny is specifically by people who were sworn to serve and obey the very authority they are now turning against. The betrayal of duty is built into the word. A mutiny is a revolt from within the ranks.
  • A riot is usually a chaotic, unplanned burst of violence, often by a crowd. A mutiny is more deliberate and organized.

Think of it this way: if citizens rise up against a king, that's a rebellion. But if the king's own soldiers and guards rise up against him, that's a mutiny.

Mutiny has always been treated as one of the most serious offenses in military and naval law. The reason is logical: an army or navy only functions because soldiers and sailors follow orders. If the very people serving in those ranks start defying or overthrowing their commanders, the entire system collapses. Because of this, mutiny has historically been punishable by extremely harsh penalties — including death — in many countries and time periods.

Even today, in most countries' military law, mutiny is a criminal offense that can result in severe punishment such as long-term imprisonment.

One of the most well-known mutinies in history is the Mutiny on the Bounty (1789). The HMS Bounty was a British naval vessel. Its crew, led by a man named Fletcher Christian, grew deeply resentful of their captain, William Bligh, whom many considered harsh and difficult. The crew eventually overpowered Captain Bligh, seized control of the ship, and set him adrift in a small boat with a handful of loyal men. This is a textbook mutiny — the captain's own crew turning against him, from within, collectively and deliberately.

In modern everyday language, people sometimes use "mutiny" loosely and humorously to describe any situation where a group of people rebel against whoever is in charge, even outside a strict military or naval setting. For example:

  • "When the coach announced an extra two hours of practice, there was nearly a mutiny among the players."
  • "The office staff staged a mutiny when the new manager banned all work-from-home days."

In these casual uses, the word is used for dramatic or humorous effect. The speaker isn't talking about a literal armed revolt — just a strong, collective pushback against authority.
How to Use "Mutiny" in a Sentence

Here are clean examples that show the noun in action:

  • "The ship's captain was powerless to stop the mutiny once the crew had made up their minds."
  • "Three officers were court-martialled for leading the mutiny."
  • "Historians still debate what drove the soldiers to mutiny."
  • "The mutiny was quickly put down, and the ringleaders were imprisoned."
Summary (The Whole Word in a Few Lines)

A mutiny is a deliberate, organized revolt by a group of subordinates — most typically soldiers or sailors — against their own commanders or the authority they were supposed to serve. It is an act of defiance from within a command structure, not an attack from outside. It implies a serious and often dangerous breakdown of authority, and is considered one of the gravest offenses in military law. In casual speech, the word is also used more lightly to describe any group standing up against whoever is in charge.
11005:
Mutism is the state or condition of being unable or unwilling to speak. A person experiencing mutism either cannot produce speech or does not speak, even though they may be fully capable of understanding language and thinking clearly.

The word is used in two overlapping ways — one broader and more everyday, and one more specific and medical.

In general use, mutism simply refers to a complete absence of speech. If someone falls utterly silent — refusing to say a single word, perhaps out of shock, grief, or stubbornness — you might describe that silence as mutism. It captures something more total and striking than just being "quiet." It implies a wall of silence, whether chosen or not.

This is where mutism is most precisely and carefully used. In medicine and psychology, mutism refers to a condition where a person does not speak, and this silence is connected to a psychological, neurological, or developmental cause — not merely a choice or preference.

Here, it matters why the person isn't speaking, because the cause shapes the type of mutism:

1. Selective Mutism

This is one of the most well-known and discussed types, especially in children.

A child with selective mutism can speak — they speak perfectly well in certain comfortable settings, like at home with family. But in other settings — such as school, with strangers, or in social situations — they become completely unable to speak, even if they want to.

This is not shyness, stubbornness, or defiance. It is an anxiety disorder. The anxiety is so intense in certain situations that it essentially "freezes" their ability to speak. They may nod, point, whisper to a trusted person, or communicate in other ways — but spoken words simply won't come out.

The key insight here: the child isn't choosing to be difficult. Speech in those anxiety-triggering situations becomes genuinely impossible for them in that moment, the same way extreme fear might make someone freeze and be unable to move.

Selective mutism usually appears in early childhood (ages 2–5 are common) and, if treated with the right support — typically therapy focused on reducing anxiety — it can often be overcome.

2. Neurological or Physical Mutism

This type occurs when the brain or body is physically damaged in a way that removes the ability to produce speech. For example:

  • A stroke or traumatic brain injury affecting the speech-producing areas of the brain can leave a person mute.
  • Severe damage to the vocal cords can physically prevent sound.

Here, the person may desperately want to speak but simply cannot. The hardware, so to speak, has been damaged.

3. Akinetic Mutism

This is a specific and unusual neurological condition where a person appears to be awake and aware but shows almost no voluntary movement or speech. They seem "present" but unresponsive — not asleep, not unconscious, yet not communicating. It is usually caused by damage to certain parts of the brain and is considered a disorder of both movement and speech together.

4. Mutism in Other Conditions

Mutism can also appear as part of broader conditions:

  • Catatonia (a state linked to severe psychiatric illness or brain disorders) can include complete mutism as one of its features.
  • Severe depression can sometimes lead to mutism, where a person is so withdrawn that they stop speaking altogether.
  • Autism spectrum disorder — some autistic people are non-speaking or have significantly limited speech, which is sometimes described using the language of mutism, though this is a more nuanced area.
  • Trauma — in rare and extreme cases, a severe traumatic experience can cause a person to stop speaking suddenly. This is sometimes called psychogenic mutism, meaning the cause is psychological rather than physical.

It helps to know what mutism is distinct from:

  • Deafness or being hard of hearing — a deaf person may not use spoken language, but that is not mutism. Mutism specifically refers to the absence of speech in someone who would otherwise be expected to speak.
  • Aphasia — this is a condition (usually from brain injury) where a person loses the ability to use language altogether — not just speech, but understanding words, reading, and writing too. Mutism is narrower: it refers specifically to the absence of speech, while other language abilities may remain intact.
  • Being shy or introverted — shyness is a personality trait. Mutism, in the medical sense, is a condition. A shy person speaks less; a person with selective mutism in certain situations literally cannot get the words out, no matter how hard they try.

Whether we're talking about a child frozen with anxiety in a classroom, an adult who has lost speech after a stroke, or someone who has gone completely silent after a trauma — what connects all uses of mutism is this: the expected flow of speech has stopped. Something — whether anxiety, injury, neurological disruption, or psychological shock — has broken the bridge between thought and spoken word.

Mutism is not simply being quiet. It is a meaningful, often profound absence of speech that signals something significant is happening in the person's mind, brain, or emotional world.
11006:
A mutt is a dog that is a mix of two or more different breeds — or whose breed is simply unknown. It does not belong to any single, recognized dog breed. Its parents (or grandparents, or further ancestors) were from different breeds, which means the dog itself is a blend of many.

For example, if a Golden Retriever and a Poodle had puppies, and those puppies then had puppies with a Labrador, the resulting dogs would be mutts — you cannot cleanly say "this is a Golden Retriever" or "this is a Poodle." It is a mix, and that mix is what makes it a mutt.

To fully understand "mutt," you need to know its opposite — a purebred dog. A purebred dog has parents, grandparents, and ancestors that all belong to the same breed. A purebred German Shepherd, for instance, has an unbroken family line of German Shepherds. It has papers, documented ancestry, and predictable traits.

A mutt has none of that. Its family tree is a mixed-up tangle of many different breeds. This is why mutts are also called mixed-breed dogs in more formal language. Another word you may see is mongrel, which means the same thing, but sounds harsher and more negative in tone.

This depends on context, but generally no — especially in modern usage. The word sits comfortably between neutral and affectionate.

Many dog owners call their beloved pets "my little mutt" or "our mutt" with nothing but warmth and love. The word often carries a kind of charm — mutts are widely seen as scrappy, resilient, loveable underdogs (quite literally). You will hear people proudly say, "She's just a mutt we rescued from the shelter" — and mean it as something sweet and wonderful.

However, in certain older or more formal contexts, or when said with a sharp tone, "mutt" can sound dismissive, suggesting the dog is of low status compared to an expensive, pedigreed breed. So tone of voice and context matter.

It's worth knowing that mutts are not considered inferior — in fact, the opposite is often true. Because mutts inherit genes from many different breeds, they tend to have greater genetic diversity, which can make them healthier and less prone to the hereditary diseases that purebred dogs often suffer from. This is informally called "hybrid vigor." Many animal shelters are full of mutts, and adopting one is considered a compassionate and popular choice.

In informal, somewhat old-fashioned American slang, "mutt" can also refer to a person — usually meaning someone who is foolish, dull, or not very impressive. Think of it like calling someone a "dummy" or a "knucklehead."

For example: "Don't listen to that mutt, he doesn't know what he's talking about."

This usage is mild in terms of offensiveness, but it is still an insult. It is not very common in everyday modern speech, but you may encounter it in older American films, crime dramas, or literature. If you hear it used for a person, the speaker is being dismissive or mocking, suggesting the person lacks intelligence or value — drawing from the same underlying idea as the dog meaning: something of uncertain, low, or mixed quality.

—What it means
Primary meaningA dog of mixed or unknown breed; not a purebred
Tone (for dogs)Neutral to affectionate; often used lovingly
Secondary meaningA foolish or unimpressive person (informal, somewhat dated)
Tone (for people)Mildly insulting or dismissive

• "We don't know exactly what breed he is — he's just a happy little mutt."
  • "She fell in love with a scruffy mutt at the shelter and brought him home the same day."
  • "That mutt has some Beagle in him, maybe some Terrier too — hard to say."
  • (Slang, for a person) "Pay no attention to that mutt — he's always getting things wrong."

In short, if someone calls a dog a mutt, picture a loveable, mixed-up blend of breeds with no papers and no pedigree — just a dog being a dog. And if someone calls a person a mutt, they're saying that person is a bit of a fool.
11007:
To mutter means to say something in a very low, quiet voice that is hard for others to clearly hear or understand. When someone mutters, the words come out softly and often unclearly — almost as if the person is speaking more to themselves than to anyone around them.

Think of it this way: when you mutter, you are not silent, but you are not really speaking out loud either. You are somewhere in the middle — words are coming out of your mouth, but they are quiet, half-formed, and swallowed.
The Most Important Thing to Know: Muttering Has an Emotion

This is what makes "mutter" special and different from just "speak quietly." Muttering is almost always tied to a negative emotion — annoyance, frustration, anger, dissatisfaction, or discontent. People mutter when they are unhappy about something but either do not want to say it directly, do not have the courage to say it loudly, or feel it is pointless to say it at all. So they say it — but only just barely.

Imagine a student who gets extra homework right before a holiday. He is unhappy, but he does not want to argue with his teacher. So as he walks out of class, he quietly says to himself, "This is so unfair." That quiet, grumbling complaint to himself — that is muttering.

• "I can't believe this," she muttered as she read the bad news.
  • He muttered something under his breath and then walked away angrily.
  • The soldier muttered a few complaints but followed the orders anyway.
  • "These shoes are killing me," she muttered to herself after walking for an hour.
  • He sat in the corner, muttering about how nobody ever listened to him.

In every example above, notice that the person is unhappy and their words are not meant to start a real conversation — they are just letting out frustration quietly.

The phrase "mutter under your breath" is extremely common in English and you will see it often. It means to say something so quietly that almost nobody else can hear it — particularly something you are grumbling about. This phrase emphasizes that the words are being kept private on purpose, usually out of frustration.

  • After being scolded by his boss, he muttered under his breath all the way back to his desk.
How You Can Use It Grammatically

Without an object (just the act of muttering):

  • He muttered to himself for a while, then went quiet.
  • She muttered under her breath and ignored him.

With an object (muttering specific words or things):

  • She muttered a quick apology and left.
  • He muttered something I couldn't quite catch.

With a direct quote (telling the reader exactly what was muttered):

  • "This is a waste of time," he muttered.

Note that when you include the actual words being muttered, the verb works just like "said" — the quoted words come before or after it.

These words are easy to confuse with "mutter," so understanding the differences is important.

Whisper — To whisper is also to speak very quietly, but whispers are usually intentional and controlled. People whisper to keep a secret, to avoid disturbing others, or to share something privately. There is nothing necessarily negative about whispering — it can be warm, playful, or conspiratorial. Muttering, on the other hand, carries frustration or discontent.

Mumble — To mumble is to speak in a way that is unclear and hard to understand, often because the speaker barely opens their mouth. Mumbling is more about poor clarity of speech than about emotion. A shy person might mumble. Someone with food in their mouth might mumble. Muttering is about speaking quietly out of frustration; mumbling is just about speaking unclearly.

Murmur — A murmur is a soft, gentle, continuous sound. It is often pleasant or soothing — the murmur of a stream, or a mother murmuring a lullaby. Muttering is disgruntled and brief; murmuring is soft and often continuous or even beautiful.

Grumble — To grumble is very close to mutter in meaning and feeling — both involve complaint and discontent. The difference is that grumbling focuses on the content (the act of complaining) while muttering focuses on the manner (the low, quiet, barely-heard voice). You can grumble loudly; you cannot mutter loudly. Also, grumbling suggests a drawn-out, ongoing complaint, while muttering tends to be brief.

Here are the most common real-life situations where muttering happens:

  • After being told off or scolded, someone might mutter as they walk away, disagreeing but not daring to speak up.
  • When something goes wrong and a person is frustrated but has no one to truly complain to, they mutter to themselves.
  • When someone disagrees with a decision but feels powerless to change it, they mutter under their breath.
  • When a person is tired, fed up, or overwhelmed, they might mutter as a way of venting silently.

To summarize everything in one clean idea: to mutter is to speak in a low, unclear, barely-audible voice, usually out of frustration, annoyance, or discontent — often to yourself or just quietly enough that others can barely hear you. It sits at the exact crossroads of "quiet" and "unhappy." That combination is what makes this word unique and gives it its very specific flavour in the English language.
11008:
Mutton is the meat of a fully grown, mature sheep — typically one that is at least two years old — prepared and eaten as food.

That's the core of it. But to truly understand mutton, you need to understand how it sits in relation to the broader world of sheep meat.
Mutton vs. Lamb — the most important distinction

Sheep are slaughtered for meat at different ages, and the age of the animal at the time of slaughter directly determines what the meat is called and how it tastes.

  • Lamb = meat from a young sheep, generally less than one year old. It is pale pink, very tender, mild and delicate in flavour.
  • Hogget = meat from a sheep between roughly one and two years old. A middle stage — used mainly in British, Australian, and New Zealand English.
  • Mutton = meat from a sheep that is two years or older. It is a deep red, has a bold and rich flavour, and is noticeably tougher.

So mutton is simply the "adult" or "older" version of lamb. The same animal, but older.
What mutton looks, smells, and tastes like

Because the sheep has had more time to grow, move around, and develop, its meat is significantly different from lamb:

  • Colour: Mutton is a deep, dark red — noticeably darker than the pale pink of lamb. This is because older muscles contain more myoglobin (a protein that stores oxygen), which gives the meat its dark colour.
  • Flavour: Mutton has a strong, rich, gamey flavour. It is much more intense and robust than lamb. Some people find this deep flavour wonderful; others find it overpowering if they are accustomed to milder meats.
  • Fat: Mutton has more fat than lamb, and that fat has a stronger smell and taste. This fat is what contributes significantly to mutton's distinctive aroma when it is being cooked.
  • Texture: Because the muscles of an older animal are more developed and worked, mutton is tougher and firmer than lamb. It does not become tender easily or quickly.

Because mutton is tough, it almost always requires slow, low-heat cooking with moisture. Rushing the cooking process results in chewy, unpleasant meat. The most common methods are:

  • Slow braising or stewing — cooking the meat in liquid (water, stock, or sauce) over a long time, usually one to three hours, until it becomes tender and falls apart.
  • Pressure cooking — a faster way to achieve the same tenderness by using high-pressure steam.
  • Slow roasting — cooking in an oven at a low temperature for several hours.

When cooked properly through slow methods, mutton becomes incredibly tender, and its strong flavour infuses the entire dish, making it deeply satisfying. This is precisely why mutton is the preferred meat in slow-cooked dishes — the long cooking time that is required to soften the meat also allows it to absorb and release flavours beautifully.

Mutton is especially popular in cuisines that favour bold, slow-cooked preparations:

  • Mutton curry — widely eaten across South Asia and the Middle East
  • Mutton biryani — a rice dish slow-cooked with mutton, spices, and herbs
  • Mutton stew — a thick, hearty broth with vegetables
  • Mutton rogan josh — a rich Kashmiri curry
  • Irish stew — traditionally made with mutton, potatoes, and onions
  • Mutton chops — grilled or pan-fried cuts from the rib or loin
A very important note for the Indian context

This is crucial if you are in India or familiar with Indian cooking: in everyday Indian usage, the word "mutton" almost always refers to goat meat, not sheep meat.

When an Indian restaurant, home cook, or market vendor says "mutton," they nearly always mean goat meat (which in precise culinary English is called chevon). So "mutton curry" in an Indian kitchen is, in practice, a goat curry.

This is a regional usage that has become deeply embedded in Indian English. Technically and in standard global English, mutton strictly means sheep meat. But in India, the word has been adopted to mean goat meat because goat is far more widely available and consumed there than sheep. You will almost never find actual sheep mutton in an ordinary Indian market or restaurant — it is almost always goat.

So:

  • In global/standard English: mutton = mature sheep meat
  • In Indian English (and in practice): mutton = goat meat

Keep this distinction in mind depending on the context in which you encounter the word.

Historically, mutton was one of the most commonly eaten meats in Europe, particularly Britain, because sheep were first kept for wool, and only slaughtered once they were old (past their wool-producing prime). This meant mutton — not lamb — was the standard form of sheep meat available.

Over the 20th century, however, tastes shifted toward milder, more tender meats, and lamb (the young animal) became far more popular in Western countries. Mutton fell out of fashion in much of Europe and North America.

Today, mutton remains very popular and widely eaten in:

  • South Asia (India, Pakistan, Bangladesh)
  • The Middle East
  • North Africa
  • Parts of the Caribbean

In these regions, the strong, rich flavour of mutton is not just tolerated but actively preferred, particularly in heavily spiced dishes where the boldness of the meat stands up well to intense seasonings.
An idiomatic use of the word

The phrase "mutton dressed as lamb" is a well-known English expression. It refers to an older person (particularly a woman, in its traditional usage) who dresses or behaves in a way considered more appropriate for a much younger person — trying to appear younger than they are. The metaphor comes from the literal distinction: presenting old (mutton) as if it were young (lamb). It is often used critically or mockingly, though awareness of its ageist undertone has made it less socially acceptable in modern usage.

Mutton is simply the meat of a mature, older sheep. It is darker, tougher, fattier, and far more flavourful than lamb. It requires long, slow cooking to become tender, and when cooked well, it produces some of the richest, most deeply flavoured dishes in world cuisine. In India specifically, the word is commonly used to refer to goat meat rather than sheep meat — an important practical distinction to carry with you.
11009:
Imagine a two-way road. Something travels from A to B, and the same thing travels from B back to A. That is the heart of "mutual." It means both sides equally and at the same time.

If you feel something toward someone, but they don't feel it back — it is NOT mutual.
If you feel something toward someone, AND they feel the same back toward you — it IS mutual.
Mutual describes a feeling, action, relationship, or agreement that is shared between two or more parties, with each side participating equally — not just one side.

"Mutual" carries two closely connected ideas. Knowing both gives you the complete picture.

1. "Each toward the other" — the reciprocal meaning

This is the strictest and most precise meaning. It means A does something to B, and B does the same thing to A. The action or feeling flows in both directions.

  • Mutual respect → I respect you. You respect me. Each of us respects the other.
  • Mutual love → She loves him. He loves her. The love moves in both directions.
  • Mutual dislike → They dislike each other. Not just one of them dislikes the other.

The defining feature here is toward each other. It's not just that two people happen to have the same feeling in isolation — it's that the feeling or action connects them in both directions simultaneously.

2. "Held in common" — the shared meaning

This is a slightly broader but equally valid and widely accepted meaning. Here, "mutual" simply means both parties share the same thing, without necessarily emphasizing the back-and-forth direction.

  • A mutual interest → We both care about the same topic.
  • A mutual goal → We both want the same outcome.
  • A mutual friend → Someone who is a friend to both of us.

"Their admiration was mutual."
She admired him, and he admired her. Neither one admired alone — it went both ways.

"They came to a mutual agreement."
Both sides agreed. It wasn't forced on one party. They both arrived at the same decision together.

"We have a mutual friend — David."
David is your friend, and also my friend. He is a connection we share.

"It was a mutual decision to end the partnership."
Both parties decided to end it. Not just one.

"The two countries signed a mutual defense treaty."
If one country is attacked, the other will help defend it — and vice versa. The protection flows in both directions.

"I hope we can find a solution that works to our mutual benefit."
Both sides gain something from the outcome. Neither side is being left out or taken advantage of.

These appear very often in English, so knowing them is valuable:

  • Mutual respect — Both people respect each other equally.
  • Mutual trust — Both sides trust each other.
  • Mutual understanding — Both people genuinely understand each other's position.
  • Mutual agreement — Both sides agreed; no one was pressured.
  • Mutual benefit — Both sides gain something.
  • Mutual friend / mutual acquaintance — A person known by both parties.
  • Mutual interest — A subject or activity that both people share an interest in.
  • Mutual fund — A financial product where many investors pool their money together and all share in the gains or losses. (This is a specialized, technical use.)

You will sometimes see writers use "common" where you might expect "mutual," and vice versa. Here is the precise difference:

"Common" simply means something that belongs to, or is shared by, both parties — full stop. There is no implication of direction.

"Mutual" in its strictest sense emphasizes the back-and-forth quality — A to B, and B to A.

So, for example:

  • "A common interest in music" = We both happen to like music. (A neutral, shared fact.)
  • "Mutual respect" = I respect you specifically, and you respect me specifically — the respect travels between us.

However — and this is important — in modern everyday English, "mutual" is widely and correctly used to mean "common" or "shared," especially in phrases like "mutual friend." This usage has been standard for centuries. So you will not be wrong to use it in either sense. Just know the subtle difference exists.

• It does not mean one-sided. If only one person feels something, it cannot be called mutual.
  • It does not mean "similar." Two people having the same hobby in separate lives is not mutual — unless that hobby involves or connects them.
  • It does not mean "many." Mutual typically describes two parties, or a small defined group — not a large crowd.
  • It does not mean "equal" in terms of quantity or size. It means equal participation from both sides, not necessarily equal amounts.

This is one of the most important and widely used phrases built from this word. "Mutually exclusive" means two things that cannot both be true, or cannot both exist, at the same time.

  • Being awake and being asleep are mutually exclusive. You cannot be both at once.
  • Choosing option A and choosing option B are mutually exclusive, if you can only pick one.

Here, "mutual" reinforces that the exclusion works both ways — A rules out B, and B rules out A.

Whenever you are unsure if "mutual" fits, ask yourself:

Does this go both ways — from A to B, and from B back to A?

If yes → "Mutual" fits perfectly.
If no, and it only goes one way → "Mutual" does not fit.

That single question will serve you correctly almost every time.
